questions.q: What percentage of Apex code coverage does Salesforce require org-wide before you can deploy to a production org?
questions.explain: The Apex Developer Guide requires unit tests to cover at least 75% of Apex code, with all tests passing, before deployment to production or packaging for the AppExchange.

questions.q: Which lines count toward Apex code coverage?
options: Non-test Apex application code that your tests actually execute
questions.explain: Coverage is measured against your real application logic. System.debug calls and the test classes/methods themselves are excluded from the calculation.

questions.q: A trigger that was only ever tested by inserting one record at a time passes all its tests. What risk does this leave unproven?
options: The trigger's bulk behavior with many records inserted in a single transaction is never actually exercised
There is no risk — one record is sufficient to prove any trigger correct
Single-record tests always run faster, which is the only downside
Field-level security is automatically skipped for single-record tests
questions.explain: Triggers always fire in bulk on Salesforce, even for a 'single' record — real-world imports and batch updates can hit the same trigger with hundreds of records at once, and single-record-only tests never prove that path works.

questions.q: Which annotation marks a class or method as test-only Apex code, excluded from the org's Apex code size limit?
questions.explain: @isTest is the modern annotation for test classes and test methods. The older 'testMethod' keyword still compiles but isTest is the current recommended style.

questions.q: What happens to DML changes (inserts, updates, deletes) made inside a test method once that method finishes?
options: They remain permanently in the org's data
They are queued for manual review before being committed
They are copied into a sandbox automatically
questions.explain: Salesforce automatically rolls back all DML performed inside a test method when it finishes, so tests never leave data behind or depend on existing org data.
